generated.title: Mountain rescue volunteer training
generated.directions: You will hear a radio presenter interviewing a woman called Elena who trains volunteers for a mountain rescue team. For questions 9–18, complete the sentences with a word or short phrase.
generated.setting: Radio interview about training for a mountain rescue team.
generated.script:
A: Good morning. You're listening to Mountain Rescue Monthly, and today I'm joined by Elena, who helps train new volunteers. Elena, thanks for coming in. What happens before someone is actually allowed to join the team?
B: Thanks for having me. Well, before being accepted, every applicant must pass an annual fitness test. It's demanding, but it keeps people safe on the hill, and we don't make exceptions.
A: And once they're in, what do they study indoors before they go out in all weathers?
B: In the classroom, trainees learn basic navigation — map reading, compass work, that sort of thing. We also talk through typical scenarios so nobody panics when a real call comes in.
A: Out on a call-out, how do team members stay in contact when the weather turns nasty?
B: Each volunteer carries a whistle, because shouting doesn't always work in wind or across a ridge. Radios help too, of course, but the whistle is simple and reliable.
A: Is there any formal medical training, or is that left to the ambulance service?
B: Yes, definitely. The initial course includes an accredited first aid qualification, and we refresh it regularly. You might be hours from a road, so those skills really matter.
A: What about clothing and kit — do people bring their own?
B: Outdoor equipment must be fully waterproof. People underestimate rain on exposed slopes — damp kit quickly becomes a safety problem, especially if you're waiting with a casualty.
A: When injuries are serious, how are casualties moved off the mountain?
B: If someone is badly hurt, rescuers sometimes request a helicopter. It's not every call, but on steep ground it can be the only realistic option when time is short.
A: Are team leaders paid for this work, or is it entirely voluntary?
B: No, team leaders are unpaid and work on a voluntary basis, like everyone else. They give up evenings and weekends because they care about the community.
A: Where is rope work most common — is it every rescue?
B: Ropes are used most often on steep terrain, where a slip would have serious consequences. We practise those techniques again and again until they feel automatic.
A: What conditions make rescues hardest for newer volunteers?
B: Many call-outs happen in poor visibility — fog, sleet, low cloud. You might know the area well, but you still have to move carefully and trust your training.
A: Finally, what do recruits say they gain from all this preparation?
B: Most recruits say the training gave them more confidence in the mountains. They still respect the risks, but they feel prepared to help when it counts.
A: Elena, that's been really helpful — thank you for explaining how new members are prepared.
